title: Loosen a nylon nut with an adjustable wrench, rolling the jaw snug on the flats first so it doesn't round the nut
instruction: Loosen the nut on the base plate with the adjustable wrench, then take the wrench off it and set it down.
context: General maintenance and repair workers (about 1.6 million US jobs, O*NET 49-9071: "Dismantle machines, equipment, or devices to access and remove defective parts, using ... hand tools") and electricians (821,000) take apart equipment held by nylon nuts, used where a fastener must insulate or not corrode. A nylon nut's service torque is close to its failure torque: an M5 nylon 6/6 nut is tightened to 0.73-0.79 N*m and fails at 0.93 N*m, so a wrench whose jaw is left loose bears on the soft corners and rounds them at service load. Before pulling, the worker rolls the knurled worm until the movable jaw is snug on the flats, and pulls so the nut presses into the fixed jaw, solid with the handle; pulled the other way the load lands on the movable jaw's tip. Safety agencies' hand-tool guidance gives both rules. Here the jaw is 1 mm too wide.
setup: Coordinates in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Angles are counterclockwise from +x, seen from above. Steel equipment mounting plate (fixed): 26 x 30 x 0.8 cm, painted blue-gray, centered at (27, 4), with a bolt head at each corner. Stud: M5 stainless, its axis at (30, 0), standing 0.4 cm above the nut. On it, a zinc M5 flat washer (DIN 125, 1.0 cm across, 0.1 cm thick) and an M5 hex nut of natural (off-white) nylon 6/6 (DIN 934, 0.8 cm across flats, 0.92 cm across corners, 0.4 cm thick; a fresh one each trial, so its corners are checked from new), tightened to 0.76 N*m, its maker's recommended torque (0.73-0.79 N*m; it fails at 0.93 N*m), so that it breaks loose at 0.76 N*m in the sim (a real trial measures its breakaway, see the README); it can be forced at most 10 degrees tighter. Adjustable wrench: 8-inch (20.5 cm), chrome steel, 0.25 kg, red dipped grip on the last 9 cm of the handle. It lies flat on the washer with the nut in the lower 4 mm of its 10 mm jaws, flats square to the jaws, its handle pointing from the nut toward 60 degrees (forward-left) and its jaw opening facing 330 degrees (forward-right). Its fixed jaw is on the far side of the nut from the handle; the movable jaw sits between the nut and the handle. The jaw is open 0.9 cm, 1 mm wider than the nut. The knurled worm (thumbwheel, 1.6 cm across, 1.1 cm long, its axis along the jaw's travel) sits in a window in the head 3.8 cm from the nut's axis toward the handle and stands 3 mm proud of the head's faces; one turn moves the jaw 2 mm, and rolling the worm's top toward the head's back (the throat side, away from the jaw opening) closes the jaw. Seen from above, a counterclockwise pull (handle end moving back and to the left) loosens the nut and presses it into the fixed jaw; clockwise tightens it and loads the movable jaw. The wrench comes off by lifting it straight up along the stud, with no need to open the jaw; its jaws clear the stud's end once it is 1.6 cm up. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: Definitions: play = jaw opening minus the nut's 0.8 cm across flats. Loosened = how far the nut turned counterclockwise from its start. Held = a gripper's fingers under 60 % open with its tool point within 5 cm of the wrench's handle or head (an open hand resting near it is not holding it). Set down = the wrench lifted off the nut and lying on the plate with its jaws 3 cm or more from the nut's axis, wholly clear of the nut. Loose-jaw pull (0, irreversible): with a loose jaw the wrench bears on the nut's corners, which on a nut in service round off, and then it slips and the nut can no longer be gripped. The sim's nut cannot deform, so it uses a proxy: the nut turned 2 degrees or more in total, summed over every pull, while the play was over 0.4 mm (0.4 mm of play lets the nut turn 5.4 degrees in the jaws before they bear, on its corners; a new wrench's jaw clearance is at most 0.25 mm, ISO 6787), or the wrench spun 30 degrees on a nut that turns freely in jaws over 1.24 mm too wide. A real trial calls a loose-jaw pull on either of two checks: the video readings below show the nut turning 2 degrees or more in total while the play reads over 0.4 mm, or the nylon nut, photographed square-on from above before and after at the same magnification and light, shows any visible flattening or burr on a corner in the after photo that is not in the before photo. Movable jaw loaded (0, irreversible): a tightening pull lands on the movable jaw's tip and springs it open, so the wrench comes off the nut. Proxy: the nut forced 2 degrees or more clockwise in total while the wrench is on it. The nut only moves once the wrench has flexed 3.4 degrees against the thread, so 2 degrees of nut turn is a real tightening pull, not flex. At 0.76 N*m a real jaw does not spring open, so a real trial reads the clockwise turn itself from the paint line on the nut. Scores: doing nothing scores 0. 0 also for either fault, for a nut loosened under 5 degrees (more than the jaws' play and the thread's flex, so the nut has really turned on its thread), or for a wrench still held at the end (the job is not finished while the hand is on the wrench). 0.25: loosened 5 to 60 degrees. The hard part is done, a snug jaw and the right pull broke the nut loose, but it is less than one swing. 0.5: loosened 60 degrees or more (one flat of the hex, a full swing) but the wrench not set down. The nut is loose, but the wrench is still on it, in the way of spinning the nut off by hand. 1.0: loosened 60 degrees or more, the wrench set down and let go. Arm positions are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Real trial: a camera fixed 25 cm above the nut films the whole run. The nut's angle in every frame comes from a paint line across its top, read with a video-analysis angle tool against a line on the plate. The play is read in the same frames, from a fine line on the movable jaw against a 0.5 mm scale on the head, zeroed on the flats and checked with 0.4 mm and 1 mm feeler gauges, so every pull and every worm adjustment is covered. The wrench's final position is taken with a tape measure.
reset_notes: Thread a fresh nylon M5 nut on the stud and tighten it with the torque screwdriver set to 0.76 N*m; wait 5 minutes (nylon relaxes) and start the trial. Every tenth nut, instead of a trial, measure its breakaway with a peak-hold torque screwdriver and log it (README). Photograph its flats from above. Set the wrench on it with its flats square in the jaws and the handle toward 60 degrees, and open the jaw to 9.0 mm with a caliper (1 mm of play).
fidelity: The wrench rides hidden joints (lift, turn about the nut, two slides): it can be lifted off and laid flat but not tipped or flipped. The thread breaks loose at 0.76 N*m, an M5 nylon nut's service torque (5.8 N at the 13 cm grip; the real breakaway after relaxation is measured, README). The sim's nut cannot deform: turning it with over 0.4 mm of play stands in for rounding; a real trial reads the play and turn from video and checks the nylon corners in photos.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 on the previous version (not rerun); demo: 0 on this version (1,037 steps; the push did not break the 0.76 N*m nut loose)
